opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a lot, honestly, because I'm still a student and it's something I deal with every week. My view is that it really depends on what the homework is for. If an assignment exists to make you practice a skill, like working through a proof or debugging your own code, then handing it to AI kind of defeats the purpose. You end up with a correct answer but you haven't built the muscle, and that shows up later in exams or research when the AI isn't there to bail you out.

That said, I don't think the answer is to avoid it completely. The way I use it is more like a tutor than a ghostwriter. I'll try a problem myself first, really struggle with it, and only when I'm stuck do I ask the model. Even then I try not to ask "what's the answer." I ask things like "what concept am I missing here" or "can you check whether this step is valid." That way the thinking still happens in my head.

And sometimes it's genuinely useful for things that aren't the core of the learning. If I need to format something, or I'm fighting with some library installation, letting AI handle that frees up time for the parts that actually matter.

I think the bigger question is that education itself probably has to adapt. If a homework problem can be solved perfectly by a model in ten seconds, maybe we need to rethink what we're asking students to do, focusing more on judgment, asking good questions, and understanding why something works, rather than just producing the output.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can free up time for the parts that matter, but does not state that learners must decide how to allocate the time AI saves.

r002.rationale: The response describes using AI as a tutor after trying a problem and for peripheral tasks. It does not say Su Tinghao uses AI to complete homework because other study methods are more efficient for his learning than doing the homework.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've gone back and forth on this. When ChatGPT first came out I was in that phase where I'd paste a problem set in and copy the answer, and I noticed pretty quickly that my exam scores didn't move, or they got worse. So I had to be a bit honest with myself about what homework is actually for.

The way I think about it now is: the struggle is the point. If I'm doing a math problem or writing a proof, the hard part, the part where I'm stuck and confused, that's exactly where the learning happens. If I let AI skip that for me, I've basically outsourced the only valuable part of the exercise.

So my rule is that I use AI the way I'd use a good TA. I'll try the problem first, properly, and only when I'm genuinely stuck do I ask it for a hint, not the solution. I'll say "don't give me the answer, just tell me what concept I'm missing." Or after I finish something, I'll ask it to critique my approach, point out gaps, play devil's advocate. That's incredibly useful, and it's something I couldn't easily get before, because a TA has office hours twice a week and AI is there at two in the morning.

Where I use it freely is on the stuff that isn't the learning objective. Formatting a bibliography, fixing LaTeX errors, cleaning up a paragraph I've already written. Nobody's learning anything from fighting with citation formatting.

The thing I worry about, for myself and for other students, is that it's very easy to feel like you understand something because you watched the AI explain it well. That feeling of understanding and actual understanding are not the same thing. So I test myself a lot now. Close the laptop, can I redo this from scratch? If not, I didn't learn it, I just read a nice explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help with hints and with tasks outside the learning objective, but it does not say learners should decide how to use the time AI saves.

r002.rationale: The response says Su Tinghao used to copy AI answers and then saw his exam scores stagnate or worsen. It does not say he did so because he judged other study methods more efficient for learning.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key is whether AI helps me understand something or just helps me finish it. If I’m stuck on homework, I’d rather ask for a hint or an explanation, then try the problem myself. If it gives me the whole answer straight away, it’s easy to mistake following the explanation for actually knowing how to do it.

A useful check is to close the AI and see if I can solve a similar problem on my own. If I can’t, I probably need to spend more time with the idea. And of course, I’d follow whatever rules the teacher has set for using AI.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using saved help to learn and checking understanding, but it does not state that learners must decide how to allocate time saved by AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses asking AI for hints rather than full answers, but does not say Su Tinghao uses AI to complete homework because he judges other study methods more efficient for his learning.

sol-6.1.text: I think AI can be useful for homework, but it depends on how I use it. If I just ask for an answer and copy it, I might finish faster, but I haven’t really learned anything. I’d rather try the problem myself first, then ask AI for a hint or an explanation if I get stuck. And afterward, I’d try to solve it again without help. For me, that’s the test: can I actually do it on my own?
